topic: Control: SPC, control charts and control plans

notes.front: What is statistical process control (SPC)?
notes.back: Applying statistical methods to find and control special cause variation in a process.
notes.explanation: LeanOhio’s definition targets special cause variation specifically, not every kind of variation.
notes.example: Like a smoke alarm for a process: it watches routine readings and flags the ones suggesting something new has gone wrong.
notes.source: LeanOhio, Lean Six Sigma Terminology (ver. 2), “Statistical Process Control (SPC)”, p. 14
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does a control chart show?
notes.back: A quality characteristic plotted against sample number or time, with a centre line and an upper and a lower control limit.
notes.explanation: The centre line stands for the mean value of the in-control process.
notes.example: Like a daily plot of a filling line’s average fill weight, with a line at the usual average and a boundary line above and below it.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 6.3.1 “What are Control Charts?”
notes.evidence: shows the value of the quality characteristic versus the sample number or versus time. In general, the chart contains a center line that represents the mean value for the in-control process. Two other horizontal lines, called the upper control limit ( UCL ) and the lower control limit ( LCL ), are also shown on the chart.

notes.front: In LeanOhio’s glossary, what is a stable process?
notes.back: A process with no assignable causes present: in other words, one in statistical control.
notes.explanation: The glossary treats “stable” and “in statistical control” as the same condition.
notes.example: Like a bus route whose journey times vary a little every day but never jump because of a road closure or a breakdown.
notes.source: LeanOhio, Lean Six Sigma Terminology (ver. 2), “Stable Process”, p. 13
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are the Western Electric (WECO) rules?
notes.back: General rules for detecting out-of-control or non-random situations on a control chart.
notes.explanation: WECO is short for Western Electric Company Rules.
notes.example: Like tripwires at different heights: one very high point, or several fairly high points in a short run, sets off the alarm.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 6.3.2 “What are Variables Control Charts?”
notes.evidence: General rules for detecting out of control or non-random situaltions WECO stands for Western Electric Company Rules

notes.front: What does an X-bar and R chart plot?
notes.back: Subgroup averages on the X-bar chart, and subgroup ranges on the R chart, which tracks process variability.
notes.explanation: The sample range is related to the process standard deviation, so the R chart can control variability.
notes.example: Like measuring a few parts every hour, then plotting their average on one chart and their largest-minus-smallest spread on another.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 6.3.2.1 “Shewhart X-bar and R and S Control Charts”
notes.evidence: This chart controls the process variability since the sample range is related to the process standard deviation.

notes.front: What does an X-bar and S chart use in place of subgroup ranges?
notes.back: Subgroup standard deviations (s), plotted on an s chart beside the chart of subgroup averages.
notes.explanation: The handbook finds the range approach satisfactory up to about 10 per sample, and subgroup standard deviations preferable for larger samples.
notes.example: Like an X-bar and R chart for a bottling line, but with the spread of each subgroup measured as a standard deviation instead of a range.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 6.3.2.1 “Shewhart X-bar and R and S Control Charts”
notes.evidence: In general, the range approach is quite satisfactory for sample sizes up to around 10. For larger sample sizes, using subgroup standard deviations is preferable.

notes.front: What is an individuals and moving range (I-MR) chart for?
notes.back: Single measurements (sample size 1): it plots each individual value and the moving range between successive values.
notes.explanation: The moving range of two successive observations is what measures process variability on this chart.
notes.example: Like logging one reading per batch of paint, and charting both each reading and how far it moved from the one before.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 6.3.2.2 “Individuals Control Charts”
notes.evidence: Control charts for individual measurements, e.g., the sample size = 1, use the moving range of two successive observations to measure the process variability.

notes.front: What does a CUSUM chart plot?
notes.back: The cumulative sum of each sample mean’s deviation from the in-control mean, Sₘ = Σ(x̄ᵢ − μ̂₀), plotted against sample number m.
notes.explanation: While the process stays in control the plotted sums wander randomly about zero; if the mean shifts upwards they drift upwards, and downwards if it falls.
notes.example: Like keeping a running total of how far each week’s average delivery time sits from the usual average, so a small, steady slip piles up.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 6.3.2.3 “CUSUM Control Charts”
notes.evidence: and compute the mean of each sample. Then the cumulative sum (CUSUM) control chart is formed by plotting one of the following quantities

notes.front: What statistic does an EWMA chart monitor?
notes.back: The exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA): an average giving less and less weight to data further back in time.
notes.explanation: Every earlier point still counts, but its influence fades the further back in time it lies.
notes.example: Like a running course mark in which recent tests count most and older tests count progressively less.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 6.3.2.4 “EWMA Control Charts”
notes.evidence: The Exponentially Weighted Moving Average (EWMA) is a statistic for monitoring the process that averages the data in a way that gives less and less weight to data as they are further removed in time.

notes.front: When are attribute control charts used instead of charts of measurements?
notes.back: When a quality characteristic cannot be expressed as a number, or doing so is impractical, so items are classified or counted.
notes.explanation: Each inspected item is sorted into one of two “buckets”, such as conforming or nonconforming.
notes.example: Like marking each invoice as correct or wrong instead of measuring anything about it.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 6.3.3 “What are Attributes Control Charts?”
notes.evidence: If we cannot represent a particular quality characteristic numerically, or if it is impractical to do so, we then often resort to using a quality characteristic to sort or classify an item that is inspected into one of two "buckets".

notes.front: What does a p chart plot?
notes.back: The proportion (fraction) of defective product in each sample.
notes.explanation: The p stands for proportion.
notes.example: Like plotting the share of each day’s parcels that arrive damaged.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 6.3.3 “What are Attributes Control Charts?”
notes.evidence: Control charts dealing with the proportion or fraction of defective product are called p charts (for proportion) .

notes.front: What does an np chart plot?
notes.back: The number of items with a yes/no outcome, such as defectives, in each subgroup, where every subgroup is the same size.
notes.explanation: MoreSteam bases its limits on the binomial distribution, which assumes every item has just two possible outcomes, such as pass or fail.
notes.example: Like counting how many of the 40 loan files checked each week are missing a signature, when exactly 40 are always checked.
notes.source: MoreSteam, “np Chart Tutorial”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does a c chart plot?
notes.back: The number (count) of defects, or nonconformities.
notes.explanation: The c stands for count.
notes.example: Like counting the blemishes found on each roll of fabric.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 6.3.3 “What are Attributes Control Charts?”
notes.evidence: Control charts dealing with the number of defects or nonconformities are called c charts (for count) .

notes.front: What does a u chart plot?
notes.back: Defects per unit: the average number of nonconformities per unit of product.
notes.explanation: The u stands for unit.
notes.example: Like tracking the average number of typing errors per page across each week’s reports.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 6.3.3 “What are Attributes Control Charts?”
notes.evidence: There is another chart which handles defects per unit , called the u chart (for unit). This applies when we wish to work with the average number of nonconformities per unit of product.

notes.front: What is a control plan?
notes.back: The central document that keeps track of the status of every significant process characteristic.
notes.explanation: MoreSteam’s version is a table whose columns, such as chart type, sampling plan and reaction plan, can be changed to suit the user.
notes.example: Like a fleet’s maintenance sheet listing, for each vehicle part, what is checked, how often, and what to do when a check fails.
notes.source: MoreSteam, “Control Plan”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does a reaction plan tell the person plotting a control chart?
notes.back: What to do when a point is out of control or out of specification.
notes.explanation: The control plan points to it by reference number, and one reaction plan may serve a family of processes of similar criticality.
notes.example: Like a laminated card beside a machine saying who to call and what to set aside when a reading breaks a limit.
notes.source: MoreSteam, “Control Plan”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In LeanOhio’s glossary, what does a standard operating procedure (SOP) contain?
notes.back: Everything for one specific operation: each step in it and about how long each step takes.
notes.explanation: The glossary defines it at the level of a single operation, with steps and approximate times as its content.
notes.example: Like a card by a laboratory bench listing each step of a test and roughly how many minutes each step takes.
notes.source: LeanOhio, Lean Six Sigma Terminology (ver. 2), “Standard Operating Procedures”, p. 14
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In control charting, what happens in Phase I?
notes.back: Initial limits are computed from historical data; points outside are investigated, some perhaps discarded, and the limits recomputed.
notes.explanation: The word “perhaps” matters: investigated points are not automatically thrown out, and the cycle repeats if they are.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 6.1.2 “What are Process Control Techniques?”
notes.evidence: we use historical data to compute the initial control limits. Then the data are compared against these initial limits. Points that fall outside of the limits are investigated and, perhaps, some will later be discarded. If so, the limits would be recomputed and the process repeated. This is referred to as Phase I.

notes.front: What is Phase II of control charting?
notes.back: Real-time process monitoring using the limits fixed at the end of Phase I.
notes.explanation: Phase II sets no new limits; it applies the ones Phase I settled.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 6.1.2 “What are Process Control Techniques?”
notes.evidence: Real-time process monitoring, using the limits from the end of Phase I, is Phase II.

notes.front: If every point on a control chart is inside the limits, is the process necessarily in control?
notes.back: Not necessarily. If the points look non-random, showing some systematic behaviour, something is still wrong.
notes.explanation: Being inside the limits is not enough on its own; a systematic pattern still calls for a look.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 6.3.1 “What are Control Charts?”
notes.evidence: Does this mean that when all points fall within the limits, the process is in control? Not necessarily. If the plot looks non-random, that is, if the points exhibit some form of systematic behavior, there is still something wrong.

notes.front: Using only the standard rule (a point beyond the 3-sigma limits), how often do false alarms occur on average?
notes.back: About once every 371 points.
notes.explanation: The handbook ties this figure to the average run length.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 6.3.2 “What are Variables Control Charts?”
notes.evidence: When following the standard Shewhart "out of control" rule (i.e., signal if and only if you see a point beyond the plus or minus 3 sigma control limits) you will have "false alarms" every 371 points on the average (see the description of Average Run Length or ARL on the next page).

notes.front: Under the WECO rules, what is the signal in the zone beyond 3 sigma?
notes.back: Any single point beyond 3 sigma, above or below the centre line.
notes.explanation: The rule applies on both sides: above +3 sigma or below −3 sigma.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 6.3.2 “What are Variables Control Charts?”
notes.evidence: Any Point Above +3 Sigma

notes.front: Under the WECO rules, how many recent points beyond 2 sigma on one side signal out of control?
notes.back: 2 out of the last 3 points beyond 2 sigma on the same side.
notes.explanation: The rule is drawn on both sides: 2 of 3 above +2 sigma, or 2 of 3 below −2 sigma.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 6.3.2 “What are Variables Control Charts?”
notes.evidence: 2 Out of the Last 3 Points Above +2 Sigma

notes.front: Under the WECO rules, how many recent points beyond 1 sigma on one side signal out of control?
notes.back: 4 out of the last 5 points beyond 1 sigma on the same side.
notes.explanation: The rule is drawn on both sides: 4 of 5 above +1 sigma, or 4 of 5 below −1 sigma.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 6.3.2 “What are Variables Control Charts?”
notes.evidence: 4 Out of the Last 5 Points Above +1 Sigma

notes.front: Under the WECO rules, how many consecutive points on one side of the centre line signal out of control?
notes.back: 8 consecutive points on the same side.
notes.explanation: This rule needs no sigma zone at all: only which side of the centre line the points fall.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 6.3.2 “What are Variables Control Charts?”
notes.evidence: 8 Consecutive Points on This Side of Control Line

notes.front: Which trend rule listed with the WECO rules concerns steadily rising or falling points?
notes.back: 6 points in a row trending up or down.
notes.explanation: It is one of two trend rules the handbook lists beside the zone rules.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 6.3.2 “What are Variables Control Charts?”
notes.evidence: 6 in a row trending up or down.

notes.front: Which trend rule listed with the WECO rules concerns points that zigzag?
notes.back: 14 points in a row alternating up and down.
notes.explanation: It is the second of the two trend rules the handbook lists beside the zone rules.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 6.3.2 “What are Variables Control Charts?”
notes.evidence: 14 in a row alternating up and down

notes.front: What does adding the WECO rules do to a Shewhart chart’s false alarms?
notes.back: Makes them more frequent: about once every 91.75 points on average.
notes.explanation: The handbook leaves it to the user to decide whether that price is worth paying.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 6.3.2 “What are Variables Control Charts?”
notes.evidence: Adding the WECO rules increases the frequency of false alarms to about once in every 91.75 points, on the average (see Champ and Woodall, 1987 ). The user has to decide whether this price is worth paying

notes.front: When does the handbook advise recalculating control limits?
notes.back: Only for a valid, compelling reason, for example at least 30 more data points with no known change to the process.
notes.explanation: Changing the limits often would negate the chart’s usefulness.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 6.3.2 “What are Variables Control Charts?”
notes.evidence: changing the control limits frequently would negate any usefulness. So, only change your control limits if you have a valid, compelling reason for doing so. Some examples of reasons: - When you have at least 30 more data points to add to the chart and there have been no known changes to the process

notes.front: What subgroup size does the handbook call typical for X-bar and R charts, and what is lost there by using the range?
notes.back: 4 or 5; not much is lost by using the range at those sizes.
notes.explanation: The handbook says “not much”, not “nothing”: a little efficiency is still given up against standard deviations.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 6.3.2.1 “Shewhart X-bar and R and S Control Charts”
notes.evidence: A typical sample size is 4 or 5, so not much is lost by using the range for such sample sizes.

notes.front: How are the R chart’s limits set from the average range, R̄?
notes.back: Upper limit = R̄ × D₄, centre line = R̄, lower limit = R̄ × D₃.
notes.explanation: D₃ and D₄ are factors that depend only on the subgroup size n.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 6.3.2.1 “Shewhart X-bar and R and S Control Charts”
notes.evidence: UCL & = & \bar{R} D_4 \\ \mbox{Center Line} & = & \bar{R} \\ LCL & = & \bar{R} D_3

notes.front: For subgroups of n = 2, the handbook’s table gives A₂ = {{c1::1.880}}, D₃ = 0 and D₄ = 3.267.
notes.explanation: A₂ sets the X-bar chart limits as grand mean ± A₂ × average range; D₃ and D₄ set the R chart limits.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 6.3.2.1 “Shewhart X-bar and R and S Control Charts”
notes.evidence: Factors for Calculating Limits for \(\bar{X}\) --> and \(R\) Charts \(n\) n --> \(A_2\) A 2 --> \(D_3\) D 3 --> \(D_4\) D 4 --> 2 1.880 0 3.267

notes.front: On an I-MR chart the limits are the mean ± 3 × (average moving range ÷ {{c1::1.128}}), 1.128 being d₂ for n = 2.
notes.explanation: The moving ranges are ranges of two observations, and either average may be replaced by a standard or target if one is available.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 6.3.2.2 “Individuals Control Charts”
notes.evidence: is the average of all the moving ranges of two observations. Keep in mind that either or both averages may be replaced by a standard or target, if available. (Note that 1.128 is the value of \(d_2\) for \(n = 2\).

notes.front: The EWMA weighting factor λ is usually set between {{c1::0.2 and 0.3}}, although the choice is somewhat arbitrary.
notes.explanation: The handbook itself calls the choice somewhat arbitrary, and points to published tables to help select λ.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 6.3.2.4 “EWMA Control Charts”
notes.evidence: is usually set between 0.2 and 0.3 (Hunter, 1986) although this choice is somewhat arbitrary. Lucas and Saccucci (1990) give tables that help the user select

notes.front: When the fraction nonconforming p is known, what are a p chart’s 3-sigma limits?
notes.back: p ± 3√(p(1 − p)/n), with p as the centre line.
notes.explanation: Here n is the sample size and p the fraction nonconforming.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 6.3.3.2 “Proportions Control Charts”
notes.evidence: UCL & = & p + 3\sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}} \\ \mbox{Center Line} & = & p \\ LCL & = & p - 3\sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}}

notes.front: Which distribution models defect counts on a c chart, and what does that give its limits?
notes.back: The Poisson distribution, whose mean and variance both equal c; so the limits are c ± k√c.
notes.explanation: The √c term is the standard deviation that follows from a variance of c.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 6.3.3.1 “Counts Control Charts”
notes.evidence: both the mean and the variance of this distribution are equal to \(c\). c . --> Then the \(k\)-sigma k -sigma --> control chart is

notes.front: How many subgroups does MoreSteam’s guide say to collect for an np chart?
notes.back: At least 20 subgroups, each the same size.
notes.explanation: Because the subgroup size never changes, only that one size needs recording, not a size for each subgroup.
notes.source: MoreSteam, “np Chart Tutorial”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: When a control chart shows the process out of control, what does the process engineer do?
notes.back: Looks for an assignable cause by following the out-of-control action plan tied to that chart.
notes.explanation: Out of control means rejecting the assumption that current data come from the same population as the data behind the limits.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 6.1.4 “What to do if the process is “Out of Control”?”
notes.evidence: If the process is out-of-control, the process engineer looks for an assignable cause by following the out-of-control action plan (OCAP) associated with the control chart. Out-of-control refers to rejecting the assumption that the current data are from the same population as the data used to create the initial control chart limits.

notes.front: A process must be {{c1::stable}} before it can be centred on a target value or its overall variation reduced.
notes.back: Stable.
notes.explanation: Centring and variation reduction both come after stability, not before.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 6.1.5 “What to do if “In Control” but Unacceptable?”
notes.evidence: Note that the process must be stable before it can be centered at a target value or its overall variation can be reduced.

notes.front: In MoreSteam’s control plan, what must be true before the Cp/Cpk column is filled in?
notes.back: The process must be stable: the plan’s process stability column records whether it is in statistical control.
notes.explanation: Capability indices are worked out only for a process marked as stable.
notes.source: MoreSteam, “Control Plan”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: After a Lean event, who should lead the follow-up, according to the government Lean starter kit?
notes.back: An implementation team leader connected to the process; not one of the organisation’s Lean facilitators, who own no process.
notes.explanation: The kit wants someone with enough standing and authority to clear obstacles and hold the team to its actions.
notes.source: US EPA, Lean in Government Starter Kit (Version 4.0), Chapter 6, “Identify an Implementation Team Leader”, p. 63
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What two things should every follow-up action item have, according to the government Lean starter kit?
notes.back: A named person responsible for it (an owner) and a deadline.
notes.explanation: The kit warns that events which look promising at the report-out often fail when follow-up actions are delayed or forgotten.
notes.source: US EPA, Lean in Government Starter Kit (Version 4.0), Chapter 6, “Tracking Follow-Up Actions”, p. 64
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A line takes subgroups of 5 bolts. The grand mean length is 60.0 mm and the average range is 2.0 mm. With A₂ = 0.577 and D₄ = 2.115, which limits are right?
notes.back: A: X-bar limits 60.0 ± 0.577 × 2.0; R chart upper limit 2.0 × 2.115.
notes.choices:
A) X-bar chart 58.846 to 61.154; R chart upper limit 4.23
B) X-bar chart 58.0 to 62.0; R chart upper limit 4.23
C) X-bar chart 58.846 to 61.154; R chart upper limit 2.115
D) X-bar chart 54.0 to 66.0; R chart upper limit 6.0
notes.choicesExplained: B adds and subtracts the average range itself, without A₂. C gives D₄ alone, forgetting to multiply by the average range. D uses 3 × range, which is not how the tabled factors work.
notes.explanation: For n = 5 the handbook tables A₂ = 0.577, D₃ = 0 and D₄ = 2.115, so the R chart’s lower limit here is 0.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 6.3.2.1 “Shewhart X-bar and R and S Control Charts”

notes.front: A hospital pharmacy logs one reading per day. The mean of the readings is 40.0 and the average moving range is 2.256. Where are the individuals chart’s limits?
notes.choicesExplained: A adds and subtracts the average moving range itself. B divides by 1.128 but leaves out the factor of 3. D multiplies by 3 but never divides by 1.128.
notes.explanation: Each moving range spans two observations, so the divisor is d₂ for n = 2, which is 1.128.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 6.3.2.2 “Individuals Control Charts”
notes.evidence: is the average of all the moving ranges of two observations. Keep in mind that either or both averages may be replaced by a standard or target, if available. (Note that 1.128 is the value of \(d_2\) for \(n = 2\).

notes.front: An inspector counts flaws on each glass panel. The average count per panel is 25. Where are the c chart’s 3-sigma limits?
notes.choices:
A) 20 and 30
B) 0 and 25
C) 10 and 40
D) 17.5 and 32.5
notes.choicesExplained: A uses ±√25 with no factor of 3. B puts the upper limit on the centre line, 25, and the lower limit at zero. D uses 1.5√25 instead of 3√25.
notes.explanation: The 3-sigma limits for a c chart are the average count ± 3 × its square root.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 6.3.3.1 “Counts Control Charts”
notes.evidence: We have seen that the 3-sigma limits for a \(c\) c --> chart, where \(c\) c --> represents the number of nonconformities, are given by --> $$ \bar{c} \pm 3 \sqrt{\bar{c}} \, , $$

notes.front: Each week a clinic checks exactly 60 referral letters and records how many are incomplete. Which chart fits these counts?
notes.back: B: an np chart, for counts of yes/no items in subgroups of constant size.
notes.choices:
A) c chart
B) np chart
C) X-bar and R chart
D) Individuals and moving range chart
notes.choicesExplained: A counts defects, not items classed as incomplete or complete. C and D are for measured values, not counts of classified items.
notes.explanation: Each letter has two outcomes and every weekly subgroup is the same size, which is the np chart’s case.
notes.source: MoreSteam, “np Chart Tutorial”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A paint shop counts the scratches on every door panel it finishes. Which chart plots these counts?
notes.back: D: a c chart, for the number of defects or nonconformities.
notes.choices:
A) X-bar and S chart
B) p chart
C) np chart
D) c chart
notes.choicesExplained: B plots the proportion of defective product, not a count of defects. C counts defective items in equal subgroups, not defects on an item. A is for measured values.
notes.explanation: Scratches are defects counted on each panel, and charts of defect counts are c charts.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 6.3.3 “What are Attributes Control Charts?”
notes.evidence: Control charts dealing with the number of defects or nonconformities are called c charts (for count) . Control charts dealing with the proportion or fraction of defective product are called p charts (for proportion) .

notes.front: A brewery measures the gravity of each batch once, and batches are hours apart. Which chart suits one measurement per sample?
notes.back: C: an individuals and moving range chart.
notes.choices:
A) X-bar and R chart
B) u chart
C) Individuals and moving range chart
D) p chart
notes.choicesExplained: A needs subgroups of several measurements to take a range. B and D are attribute charts, for counts and proportions.
notes.explanation: With a sample size of 1, the moving range of two successive observations measures variability.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 6.3.2.2 “Individuals Control Charts”
notes.evidence: Control charts for individual measurements, e.g., the sample size = 1, use the moving range of two successive observations to measure the process variability.

notes.front: A lab measures 20 tablets from every production run and wants a chart of averages and spread. Which pair does the handbook prefer at this size?
notes.back: D: X-bar and S, since subgroup standard deviations are preferable above about 10.
notes.choices:
A) X-bar and R chart
B) c chart
C) np chart
D) X-bar and S chart
notes.choicesExplained: A is quite satisfactory only up to about 10 per sample. B and C are attribute charts for counts, not measurements.
notes.explanation: A subgroup of 20 is beyond the size where the range approach is quite satisfactory.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 6.3.2.1 “Shewhart X-bar and R and S Control Charts”
notes.evidence: In general, the range approach is quite satisfactory for sample sizes up to around 10. For larger sample sizes, using subgroup standard deviations is preferable.

notes.front: A team suspects its process mean is creeping slowly upwards, by well under 2 sigma. Which chart is built to catch a small, gradual drift?
notes.back: B: an EWMA chart, which can be made sensitive to a small or gradual drift.
notes.choices:
A) An X-bar chart using only the 3-sigma rule
B) An EWMA chart
C) A c chart
D) A p chart
notes.choicesExplained: A reacts only when the latest point crosses a limit. D and C are attribute charts for proportions and counts, not a measured mean.
notes.explanation: The choice of weighting factor λ is what tunes the EWMA’s sensitivity to a small drift.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 6.3.2.4 “EWMA Control Charts”
notes.evidence: the EWMA control procedure can be made sensitive to a small or gradual drift in the process, whereas the Shewhart control procedure can only react when the last data point is outside a control limit.

notes.front: A process is in statistical control, but its average sits well above the customer’s target. What should the team do?
notes.back: D: use process improvement techniques, such as experiments or calibration, to bring it on target.
notes.choices:
A) Recalculate the control limits around the target
B) Follow the out-of-control action plan for an assignable cause
C) Nothing: in control means acceptable
D) Use improvement techniques such as experiments or calibration to put it on target
notes.choicesExplained: A changes the chart, not the process. B is for out-of-control signals, and none has occurred. C confuses predictable with acceptable.
notes.explanation: The handbook names experiments, calibration and re-analysis of historical data for putting a process on target or reducing variability.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 6.1.5 “What to do if “In Control” but Unacceptable?”
notes.evidence: Process improvement techniques such as - experiments - calibration - re-analysis of historical database can be initiated to put the process on target or reduce the variability.

notes.front: A team computes first control limits from last quarter’s data, and two historical points fall outside them. What should happen next?
notes.back: B: this is Phase I, so investigate the points, and recompute the limits if any are discarded.
notes.choices:
A) Start real-time monitoring with the limits unchanged
B) Investigate the two points; if any are discarded, recompute the limits
C) Delete both points at once and move straight to monitoring
D) Replace the limits with the customer’s specification limits
notes.choicesExplained: A skips the Phase I investigation. C discards points without investigating them, though only “perhaps” some are discarded. D mixes up control and specification limits.
notes.explanation: Phase I repeats compute, compare, investigate and recompute before Phase II monitoring begins.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 6.1.2 “What are Process Control Techniques?”
notes.evidence: Points that fall outside of the limits are investigated and, perhaps, some will later be discarded. If so, the limits would be recomputed and the process repeated. This is referred to as Phase I. Real-time process monitoring, using the limits from the end of Phase I, is Phase II.

notes.front: Of an X-bar chart’s last five points, four lie between +1 and +2 sigma and one just below the centre line. None is beyond 3 sigma. What do the WECO rules say?
notes.back: A: 4 of the last 5 points beyond +1 sigma is an out-of-control signal.
notes.choices:
A) A signal: 4 of the last 5 points are beyond 1 sigma on one side
B) A signal under the 2-of-3-beyond-2-sigma rule
C) A signal under the 8-in-a-row rule
D) No signal, because every point is inside the 3-sigma limits
notes.choicesExplained: D ignores every rule except the 3-sigma one. B needs points beyond 2 sigma, and none is. C needs 8 consecutive points on one side, not 4 of 5.
notes.explanation: Such a pattern is about as rare as a single point beyond 3 sigma, so it is treated as a signal.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 6.3.2 “What are Variables Control Charts?”
notes.evidence: and the probability of observing four points out of five in a row between \(1 \sigma\) --> and \(2 \sigma\) --> are also about 0.3 %.

notes.front: A call centre audits 100 calls per sample, and the known fraction nonconforming is p = 0.10. Where are the p chart’s 3-sigma limits?
notes.choicesExplained: A uses one standard error instead of three. C uses two instead of three. D multiplies by 3 without taking the square root.
notes.explanation: The standard error here is √(0.09/100) = 0.03, and three of them make 0.09.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 6.3.3.2 “Proportions Control Charts”
notes.evidence: UCL & = & p + 3\sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}} \\ \mbox{Center Line} & = & p \\ LCL & = & p - 3\sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}}

notes.front: What does each kind of limit decide: control limits and specification limits?
notes.back: Control limits: whether the process is in statistical control. Specification limits: whether the product will function as intended.
notes.explanation: Control limits concern consistent output from the process; specification limits concern whether the product works.
notes.contrast: Control limits: consistent output from the process. Specification limits: a product that works as intended.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 6.3.2 “What are Variables Control Charts?”
notes.evidence: Control Limits are used to determine if the process is in a state of statistical control (i.e., is producing consistent output). Specification Limits are used to determine if the product will function in the intended fashion.

notes.front: A supervisor wants to draw the customer’s tolerance lines on an X-bar chart and use them as its control limits. What is the flaw?
notes.back: B: specification limits judge the product; control limits judge whether the process is in statistical control.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing: control limits and tolerances are the same thing
B) Tolerances show whether the product will work, not whether the process is in statistical control
C) Tolerances may only go on a p chart
D) Control limits must always be exactly twice the tolerance
notes.choicesExplained: A is the very confusion the handbook separates. C invents a rule about chart types. D invents a fixed ratio between the two kinds of limit.
notes.explanation: The two sets of limits answer different questions, so one cannot stand in for the other.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 6.3.2 “What are Variables Control Charts?”
notes.evidence: Control Limits are used to determine if the process is in a state of statistical control (i.e., is producing consistent output). Specification Limits are used to determine if the product will function in the intended fashion.

notes.front: For what size of mean shift are CUSUM charts better than Shewhart charts?
notes.back: Shifts in the mean of 2 sigma or less.
notes.explanation: Their strength is efficiency at detecting small shifts in the mean of a process.
notes.contrast: Shewhart charts are simpler and more intuitive, but slower to catch small mean shifts.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 6.3.2.3 “CUSUM Control Charts”
notes.evidence: have been shown to be more efficient in detecting small shifts in the mean of a process. In particular, analyzing ARL's for CUSUM control charts shows that they are better than Shewhart control charts when it is desired to detect shifts in the mean that are 2 sigma or less.

notes.front: What is an out-of-control decision based on in a Shewhart chart, compared with an EWMA chart?
notes.back: Shewhart: only the most recent measurement. EWMA: a weighted average of all prior data, latest point included.
notes.explanation: Both still depend on control limits estimated from historical data.
notes.contrast: EWMA carries memory of earlier points; a Shewhart chart has none.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 6.3.2.4 “EWMA Control Charts”
notes.evidence: depends solely on the most recent measurement from the process and, of course, the degree of "trueness" of the estimates of the control limits from historical data. For the EWMA control technique, the decision depends on the EWMA statistic, which is an exponentially weighted average of all prior data, including the most recent measurement.

notes.front: How does a defect differ from a defective (nonconforming) item?
notes.back: A defect is one nonconformity; a defective item contains at least one. An item with several defects may still be conforming.
notes.explanation: A defect is a single point where a specification is not met, while “defective” is a verdict on the whole item.
notes.contrast: Defects are counted on an item; defectives are items classified as a whole.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 6.3.3.1 “Counts Control Charts”
notes.evidence: Furthermore, each chip, (e.g., the specific point) at which a specification is not met becomes a defect or nonconformity. So, a nonconforming or defective item contains at least one defect or nonconformity. It should be pointed out that a wafer can contain several defects but still be classified as conforming.
